unit.title: Perform manual metal arc welding to weld to AWS specification (Alloy steel plate)

theory1.instructions: Answer all 45 questions. Each question has one best answer: choose it. Each question is worth 1 mark. Time allowed: 2 hours 30 minutes. Your answers are saved as you go.

questions.stem: What makes a steel plate a "low-alloy" steel, and not a plain carbon steel?
options: It has less carbon than mild steel, and nothing else
Small amounts of nickel, chromium or molybdenum are added
It has been rolled much thinner than a normal structural plate
It has a zinc coating on both faces of the plate

questions.stem: Why is low-alloy plate more likely than mild steel plate to crack beside the weld?
options: Its heat-affected zone can harden as it cools
It melts at a much lower temperature than mild steel
It does not conduct the welding current as well
Its surface scale is too thick for the arc to pass

questions.stem: Using CE = C + Mn/6 + (Cr + Mo + V)/5 + (Ni + Cu)/15, what is the CE of a plate with 0.18% C, 1.2% Mn, 0.2% Cr, 0.1% Mo, 0.3% Ni and no V or Cu?
As the carbon equivalent (CE) of a plate goes up, what usually happens to the preheat the WPS asks for?
options: It goes down, as the steel is stronger
It stays the same for every CE value
It is replaced by cooling with water
It goes up, to slow the cooling

questions.stem: Two low-alloy plates have the same CE. One is 12 mm thick and the other 50 mm. Which joint needs more preheat, and why?
options: The 50 mm plate, as it draws heat from the joint faster
The 12 mm plate, as thin plate always cracks more easily
Both the same, as the preheat depends only on the CE value
Neither, as preheat is needed only on pipe joints

questions.stem: In the electrode class E8018-C1, what does the "C1" tell the welder about the weld metal?
options: It is a chromium-molybdenum weld metal
It contains about 2.5% nickel
It contains about half a percent molybdenum
It is made to match weathering steel

questions.stem: Which electrode would usually be chosen for a weathering steel plate that will be left unpainted outdoors?
An alloy job calls for E7018-A1 electrodes. Which element does the "A1" show has been added to the weld metal?
options: Nickel
Molybdenum
Chromium
Copper

questions.stem: An electrode is marked E8018-C3 H4R. What does the "R" at the end tell you?
options: It must be run on reverse (AC) polarity only
It is for root runs only, and never for the fill passes
It may be re-dried as many times as needed
Its coating has passed a test for resisting moisture

questions.stem: Hydrogen cracking needs three conditions at the same time. Which set is right?
options: Hydrogen, a hard structure, and stress
Hydrogen, a long arc, and a wide weave
Oxygen, a soft structure, and heat
Rust, a short arc, and fast travel

questions.stem: Why does the inspection plan for a low-alloy plate job wait a set time after welding before the final crack check?
options: So the weld cools enough to be safe to touch
So the slag has time to fall off by itself
Hydrogen cracks can appear hours after welding
So the weld has time to become fully hardened all through

questions.stem: A quenched and tempered high-strength plate is to be welded. Why does the WPS set a maximum heat input as well as a minimum preheat?
options: High heat input makes too much spatter on the plate
A slow, hot weld uses too many electrodes on the job
High heat input makes the slag hard to chip off
Too much heat softens the plate beside the weld

questions.stem: A quenched and tempered plate has bowed after welding. Why must it not be heated to straighten it beyond the limit the steel maker gives?
options: It will turn a different colour and look poor
It can lose the strength its heat treatment gave it
The paint will not stick to it after heating
It will become strongly magnetic and attract weld spatter

questions.stem: On a low-alloy plate procedure test, the recorder notes 24 V, 150 A and a travel speed of 150 mm/min for one fill pass. Taking heat input as V × A × 60 ÷ (speed × 1000), what figure goes on the record?
options: 0.96 kJ/mm
1.44 kJ/mm
2.16 kJ/mm
14.4 kJ/mm

questions.stem: The WPS limits heat input to 1.5 kJ/mm. A welder runs at 25 V and 160 A. What is the slowest travel speed allowed?
options: 120 mm/min
160 mm/min
200 mm/min
240 mm/min

questions.stem: Why should the preheat on a thick alloy plate be checked on the face opposite the burner, where that can be reached?
options: The far face always cools faster than the near one
The burner face always reads too low on a temperature crayon
To be sure the heat has soaked right through the plate
So the welder can start before the plate is fully hot

questions.stem: Between passes, the joint on an alloy plate is found to be hotter than the WPS's maximum interpass temperature. What should the welder do?
options: Wait until it cools into range before the next pass
Cool it quickly with a wet rag to save time on the job
Carry on, but use a smaller electrode
Weld faster so less heat goes into the pass

questions.stem: On a plate test with a backing strip, why must the strip be of the same type of steel as the alloy plate, or the type the WPS names?
options: So it can be cut off and reused on the next test
So it shows up clearly on the inspection photos
So it bends more easily than the test plate in the bend jig
It melts into the weld, so it must not spoil its make-up

questions.stem: Why is a flame-cut bevel on low-alloy plate ground back to bright metal before welding?
options: So the bevel angle can be measured more easily
So the plate is lighter and easier to lift
The cut face can be hard and may hold cracks or oxide
So the electrode does not stick to the bevel face at the start

questions.stem: Which joint is most at risk of lamellar tearing?
options: A tee joint with a large weld on the face of thick plate
A lap joint between two thin sheets with a small fillet
A butt joint in thin plate welded from both sides
A corner joint in a light angle-iron gate frame

questions.stem: Which step helps most to prevent lamellar tearing in a heavily loaded tee joint in thick plate?
options: Use the largest electrode and the highest current
Weld the joint as fast as possible and without any preheat
Use a rutile electrode instead of a low-hydrogen one
Use through-thickness tested plate and butter the face

questions.stem: Why are stringer beads, or a narrow weave, usually preferred to a wide weave on low-alloy plate?
options: They are quicker to clean between the passes
They keep the heat input within the WPS limits
They need no preheat at all, even on thick plate
They use larger electrodes at a lower current

questions.stem: In the 3G position on alloy plate with low-hydrogen electrodes, how are the fill passes normally laid?
options: Downhill, with a fast drag and no weave
Downhill on the root, uphill on the cap
Uphill, with a slight weave within the WPS width
Sideways across the joint in short dabs

questions.stem: For the root of an overhead (4G) butt on 12 mm alloy plate with a backing strip, which electrode size is usually the best choice?
options: A small size, such as 3.2 mm
The largest size, such as 6 mm
Any size, as it makes no difference
A size chosen by the store on the day

questions.stem: A low-alloy plate is to be welded to a mild steel plate. If the WPS allows, which kind of electrode is usually chosen?
options: A high-alloy stainless electrode, just to be on the safe side
A rutile electrode, for its easy-to-use arc
A cellulosic electrode, for deep penetration
A low-hydrogen one matching the mild steel's strength

questions.stem: When low-alloy plate is welded to mild steel, which plate's needs usually set the preheat?
options: The alloy plate, which is more crack-sensitive
The mild steel, as it is the weaker plate
Whichever plate is the thinner of the two
Neither: preheat is never used on such joints

questions.stem: Why might a WPS ask for the face of a crack-sensitive plate to be buttered before the joint is fitted up?
options: So the joint can be welded without any preheat
So the plate looks smoother before it is painted
So the joint is made onto a sound, tougher layer
So the welder can use a larger electrode later

questions.stem: Generally, why does an AWS plate test on 25 mm plate qualify a welder for a wider thickness range than a test on 10 mm plate?
options: Thicker plate is cheaper, so more welders can test
It proves he can control many passes and the heat
The bend strips from thick plate are easier to pass
Thick plate needs no preheat, so the test is fairer

questions.stem: On a procedure test for alloy plate, what does a transverse tensile test of the welded joint show?
options: The hydrogen level in the weld metal
How hard the cap is at its centre line
The make-up of the electrode's coating
Whether the joint is strong enough

questions.stem: Why may an alloy steel WPS call for impact (Charpy) tests on the weld metal and the heat-affected zone?
options: To prove they stay tough, not brittle, when cold
To find the exact chemistry of the weld metal
To check that the cap height is within the limit
To measure the heat input of each weld pass

questions.stem: Why might the heat-affected zone of a low-alloy plate weld be hardness tested on a procedure test?
options: Soft zones show the weld is too strong
Hardness shows how fast the welder worked
High hardness warns of a risk of cracking
Hardness tells you the electrode's size

questions.stem: A crack is found in the heat-affected zone along the cap toe of an alloy plate weld the morning after welding. What is the most likely cause?
options: Too much preheat, which made the plate far too soft at the toe
Hydrogen cracking from low preheat or damp electrodes
A short arc held for the whole of the cap
Electrodes that were kept too long in the oven

questions.stem: Small star-shaped cracks keep appearing at the end of each run on alloy plate. What is the best cure?
options: Break the arc quickly by pulling the rod away
Use a larger electrode for every pass
Turn the current up for the final cap only
Fill the crater before the arc is broken

questions.stem: Why is a joint that is heavily restrained, such as an insert plate welded into a stiff frame, more likely to crack?
options: The weld cannot shrink freely, so stress builds up
It needs less weld metal, so the bead is too thin
It is welded in the flat position, which is harder
It cools more slowly, so the steel becomes too soft

questions.stem: Low-hydrogen alloy electrodes were re-dried once, as the maker allows only one re-dry. They have now been left out in damp air again. What should be done?
options: Re-dry them again for twice as long
Use them on the root runs only
Scrap them; they must not be re-dried again
Warm them on the plate before each use

questions.stem: Why must the safety data sheet (SDS) for an alloy electrode be read before a long welding job?
options: It gives the current range for each electrode size
It lists the welder's qualifications needed for the whole job
It shows the price of the electrodes per packet
It names the harmful metals in the fume and the controls

questions.stem: An alloy plate has been preheated to 150 °C. It does not glow and looks normal. Why is that a hazard?
options: It is too cool to weld and must be reheated
It looks cold but can burn badly at a touch
It will give off toxic gas until it glows
It is likely to crack if anyone touches it

questions.stem: Low-alloy plate and mild steel plate look the same in the rack. How should the team stop them being mixed up?
options: Keep them marked, and copy heat numbers onto cut pieces
Store them together so they are easy to find
Weigh each plate before use to tell them apart
Ask the welder to judge by the colour of the scale

questions.stem: A mill certificate shows 0.25% carbon in a plate, but the WPS was qualified on plate with 0.18% carbon. What should the team leader do?
options: Weld it anyway, as carbon makes the plate stronger
Use a larger electrode to make up for the carbon
Stop and check whether the WPS still covers it
Weld it without preheat to keep it from hardening

questions.stem: Each 450 mm alloy electrode is burned down to a 50 mm stub. About what percentage of each electrode is left as stub?
The WPS says to preheat a band each side of the joint at least 3 times the plate thickness, and never less than 75 mm. How wide is the band on each side for 30 mm plate?
options: 75 mm
105 mm
180 mm
90 mm

questions.stem: A welder wants to re-tack a joint on alloy plate without preheat, "because it is only a tack". What should the team leader say?
options: That is fine, as long as the tacks are small
Tacks need the same preheat, as they can crack too
Tack it cold, then preheat before the root run
Use a rutile electrode for the tacks instead

questions.stem: Why are the preheat, interpass temperature and heat input of each pass recorded during a procedure test on alloy plate?
options: They become the PQR values that set the WPS limits
So the welder's speed can be compared with others
So the store can order the right electrodes later
So the plate can be sold with its own test sheet

questions.stem: A crack in an alloy plate weld has been gouged out. Why is the groove checked by dye penetrant or magnetic particle testing before it is re-welded?
options: To warm the groove up before the repair weld
To clean oil from the groove before welding
To mark the groove so the welder can find it
To be sure all of the crack has been removed

questions.stem: A welder has passed only a 3G groove test on alloy plate. Generally, may he weld overhead groove joints on the job?
options: Yes, a vertical test covers every position
Yes, if the overhead joints are short ones
No, 3G generally covers flat, horizontal and vertical
No, 3G covers the vertical position only and nothing else

theory2.instructions: Section A has 15 short answers (2 marks each). Section B has 10 essay questions (5 marks each): answer each in full sentences. Time allowed: 3 hours 35 minutes. Your answers are saved as you go.

shortAnswers.stem: When judging how likely a steel is to harden and crack after welding, what do the letters CE stand for?
In the carbon equivalent formula, which element is counted at its full percentage, without being divided?
Which alloying element is added to the weld metal of the "C" group of electrodes, such as E8018-C1 and E8018-C3?
What is the name of the cracking that runs in steps parallel to the surface of a thick plate, under a large tee-joint weld?
A low-alloy plate is 25 mm thick. The WPS preheat table gives 75 °C for plate up to 20 mm and 110 °C for plate over 20 mm. What preheat is needed, in °C?
What is the welding term for laying weld metal on a joint face before the joint is fitted up?
What is the name of the impact test in which a notched bar of weld metal is broken by a swinging hammer?
Which kind of test, made by pressing a diamond or a hard ball into a polished section, shows whether the heat-affected zone has become too hard?
A high-strength plate is made by heating it, cooling it fast in water, then reheating it to a lower temperature. What is this kind of plate called (three words)?
An electrode is 450 mm long and is burned down to a 50 mm stub. How many millimetres of the electrode are used?
On a procedure test, a recorder times a 240 mm long run at 1.5 minutes. What is the travel speed, in mm/min?
What is the name of the technique in which each later bead is placed so that its heat softens the heat-affected zone of the beads before it?
What name is given to the low-alloy steel, often left unpainted on bridges, that forms a tight rust layer which protects it?
An electrode is marked E8018-C3 H4R. What is the most diffusible hydrogen its weld metal may have, in mL per 100 g?
What is the name of the hard, brittle structure that can form in the heat-affected zone of alloy steel when it cools too fast?

essays.stem: Explain how hydrogen cracking happens in welds on low-alloy steel plate, how each of its causes is controlled, and why final inspection is often delayed after welding.
essays.modelAnswer: Hydrogen cracking needs three things at once: hydrogen in the weld, a hard, crack-sensitive structure in the weld or heat-affected zone, and stress. Hydrogen comes from moisture in electrode coatings, damp air, rust, oil and paint on the joint. It is controlled by using low-hydrogen electrodes stored and re-dried as the maker says, kept in a heated quiver, and by cleaning the joint. A hard structure forms when alloy steel cools quickly. Preheat and a suitable heat input slow the cooling so the zone is softer and hydrogen can escape. Stress comes from shrinkage and restraint. It is reduced with good fit-up, a balanced sequence and no over-welding. Hydrogen moves through the steel for hours after welding, so a crack may only form later. For this reason the plan often waits a set time, as the code or WPS says, before the final crack check.
markingPoints: Names the three conditions: hydrogen, hard structure, stress
Hydrogen control: low-hydrogen electrodes stored and re-dried, clean joints
Hard structure control: preheat and heat input slow the cooling
Stress control: fit-up, sequence, no over-welding
Explains delayed cracking and the waiting time before final inspection

essays.stem: Explain how carbon equivalent, plate thickness and restraint are used to decide the preheat for a joint in alloy steel plate. Include a worked CE example.
essays.modelAnswer: Carbon equivalent (CE) puts the effect of carbon and the alloying elements into one number. A common formula is CE = C + Mn/6 + (Cr + Mo + V)/5 + (Ni + Cu)/15. For a plate with 0.18% C, 1.2% Mn, 0.2% Cr, 0.1% Mo and 0.3% Ni, CE = 0.18 + 0.20 + 0.06 + 0.02 = 0.46. The higher the CE, the more easily the heat-affected zone hardens, so more preheat is needed. Thickness matters because thick plate draws heat out of the joint faster, so the joint cools quicker; a 50 mm plate needs more preheat than a 12 mm plate with the same CE. A highly restrained joint cannot shrink freely and has more stress, so it also needs more care. The welder takes the CE from the mill certificate, then uses the WPS or the code's preheat table with the thickness and hydrogen level, and never sets less preheat than the WPS gives.
markingPoints: Explains what CE is and gives the formula
Correct worked example
Higher CE: more hardening, more preheat
Thicker plate and higher restraint: more preheat or care
Uses the mill certificate and the WPS or code table; never below WPS

essays.stem: Describe how you would weld a single-V butt test in low-alloy steel plate in the vertical position (3G) with low-hydrogen electrodes, from receiving the plates to handing them in for bend testing.
essays.modelAnswer: I check the plate marking and heat number against the mill certificate and the WPS, and check the electrodes are the class on the WPS and come from the holding oven. I grind the bevels to bright metal, set the root opening on a backing strip of the steel the WPS names, and tack at the ends. I preheat evenly over the band the WPS gives, and check the temperature with a crayon or contact thermometer, including before each tack. I weld uphill with a short arc: a root fused into both bevels and the backing, then fill passes with a slight weave no wider than the WPS allows, chipping and brushing each pass, filling every crater. I check the interpass temperature before each pass and record the current, voltage, run length and time so heat input can be worked out. The cap is flat and even. I let the plate cool as the WPS says, inspect it visually after the set waiting time, and hand it in with the record.
markingPoints: Checks plate and electrodes against the mill certificate and WPS
Prepares bevels, backing and root opening; tacks with preheat
Preheat applied evenly and checked; interpass checked before each pass
Uphill technique, short arc, weave within limits, cleaning and crater filling
Records data for heat input; slow cooling, delayed visual check, hand-in with record

essays.stem: Compare welding a quenched and tempered high-strength plate with welding an ordinary low-alloy structural plate. Cover heat input, preheat, technique and what goes wrong if the limits are not kept.
essays.modelAnswer: Both plates need low-hydrogen electrodes and enough preheat to stop hydrogen cracking. On an ordinary low-alloy plate, the main worry is cooling too fast, so the WPS gives a minimum preheat, and higher heat input is usually helpful. A quenched and tempered plate gets its strength from heat treatment. If it is heated too much, the zone next to the weld is softened and loses strength and toughness. So its WPS gives a minimum and a maximum preheat and interpass temperature, and a maximum heat input. The welder uses stringer beads or a narrow weave, small electrodes and steady travel, and checks heat input from the volts, amps and speed. Too little heat gives hard, cracked zones, while too much gives soft, weak zones. Heat straightening is also limited on quenched and tempered plate. On both plates the welder follows the WPS exactly and records the values.
markingPoints: Both need low-hydrogen electrodes and minimum preheat
Ordinary low-alloy: main risk is fast cooling and hardening
Q&T: maximum preheat, interpass and heat input to avoid softening
Technique: stringer beads, narrow weave, heat input checked
Effects of too little and too much heat; follow and record the WPS

essays.stem: Explain what heat input is, how it is worked out on a welding procedure test, and why it matters on alloy steel plate. Give a worked example.
essays.modelAnswer: Heat input is the amount of arc energy put into each millimetre of weld. It is found from heat input (kJ/mm) = volts × amps × 60 ÷ (travel speed in mm/min × 1000). On a procedure test, a recorder notes the current and voltage with a meter, and times each run and measures its length to get the travel speed. For example, 24 V and 150 A over a 300 mm run made in 2 minutes is 150 mm/min, giving 24 × 150 × 60 ÷ 150 000 = 1.44 kJ/mm. It matters because low heat input with fast cooling can leave a hard, crack-prone heat-affected zone, while high heat input can soften quenched and tempered plate and lower the toughness of the weld. The heat inputs recorded on the procedure test go on the PQR and set the limits on the WPS, so production welders must stay within them.
markingPoints: Defines heat input as arc energy per length of weld
Gives the formula correctly
Explains how volts, amps, run length and time are measured on the test
Correct worked example
Explains effects of too low and too high heat input and the link to PQR/WPS limits

essays.stem: Explain how a welder chooses MMAW electrodes for alloy steel plate work. Cover strength, the alloy group, hydrogen level, and joints between alloy plate and mild steel.
essays.modelAnswer: The electrode must be the class the WPS names. The first figures show the weld metal strength, for example 80 in E8018 means about 80 000 psi, which must match the plate. The suffix shows the alloy group: C1 or C3 for nickel steels used where toughness in the cold matters, A1 for carbon-molybdenum, W for weathering steel, so the weld rusts to the same colour, and M for high-strength military-type grades. The 18 shows a low-hydrogen, all-position iron powder coating. The H4 or H8 mark shows the hydrogen level, and R shows the coating resists moisture; lower hydrogen is chosen for higher strength or thicker plate. For an alloy plate joined to mild steel, the WPS usually calls for a low-hydrogen electrode matching the weaker mild steel, with preheat set for the alloy side. The welder checks the class on every packet before use.
markingPoints: Uses the class named on the WPS
Strength figures matched to the plate
Alloy suffix groups explained (C, A, W or M) with a use for each
Hydrogen designator and R explained
Dissimilar joint: low-hydrogen electrode matching the mild steel, preheat for the alloy side

essays.stem: Describe how a welding procedure for MMAW of alloy steel plate is qualified to the AWS code the Centre uses, and the tests that may be done on the test plate.
essays.modelAnswer: First a draft procedure is written, giving the plate, joint, electrode, positions, preheat, interpass and heat input range. A skilled welder then welds a test plate to it while an inspector watches and records the actual values: the plate's heat number, electrode lot, preheat, interpass temperatures, current, voltage and travel speed for each pass. After any waiting time, the plate is visually inspected and may be tested by radiography or ultrasonics. Test pieces are then cut from set places. Transverse tensile tests show the joint's strength. Bend tests show ductility and fusion. A macro etch shows fusion and penetration, and hardness tests on the heat-affected zone show any risk of cracking. Charpy impact tests may be needed where the job needs toughness in the cold. If all pass, the results are written on the procedure qualification record (PQR), and the WPS is issued with limits taken from it.
markingPoints: Draft procedure with the main variables
Test plate welded and actual values recorded by an inspector
Visual and non-destructive testing first
Mechanical tests named with purpose: tensile, bend, macro, hardness, Charpy
Results recorded on the PQR; WPS limits taken from it

essays.stem: Describe lamellar tearing and restraint cracking in thick alloy steel plate fabrications, and explain how design, material choice and welding sequence help to prevent them.
essays.modelAnswer: Lamellar tearing is cracking under a weld in thick plate, running in steps parallel to the plate surface. It happens when a large weld on the face of a plate pulls on it through its thickness, where flat inclusions make the steel weak. Restraint cracking happens when a weld in a stiff joint cannot shrink freely, so stress builds up and cracks the weld or the heat-affected zone. Design helps by avoiding large welds that pull through the thickness, using the smallest weld size that is strong enough, and arranging joints so the load is not across the plate thickness. Material choice helps by using plate tested for through-thickness properties where the drawing calls for it. Welding helps by buttering the face with a tougher layer, using low-hydrogen electrodes and correct preheat, and a sequence that lets parts shrink freely, welding the most restrained joints first and balancing the heat.
markingPoints: Describes lamellar tearing and its cause (through-thickness pull, inclusions)
Describes restraint cracking (shrinkage stress in a stiff joint)
Design measures: smaller welds, joint layout
Material: through-thickness tested plate
Welding: buttering, low hydrogen, preheat, sequence that allows shrinkage

essays.stem: Describe the hazards of preheating and MMAW welding of alloy steel plate in the Centre's workshop, and the controls you would use for each.
essays.modelAnswer: Alloy electrodes can give off fume containing manganese, nickel or chromium, so I would read the SDS, use extraction close to the arc and give respirators where it is not enough. Preheated plate at 150 °C or more does not glow but burns badly, so it is marked hot, handled with tongs and heat-resistant gloves, and fenced off. Gas preheating burners need checked hoses, flashback arrestors, a clear area and an extinguisher, and hoses must be kept away from the hot plate. Electric heating pads are set up only by a trained person. The arc needs screens, the correct shade and dry PPE, and welders must not stand on wet floors. Thick alloy plates are heavy, so they are lifted with the right gear and slings, not by hand. Long hot work in hot weather needs water and rest breaks. All work follows the maker's instructions and the Centre's rules.
markingPoints: Fume: SDS, extraction, respirators
Hot plate: mark, tongs, gloves, barriers
Gas preheating: hoses, arrestors, fire control; electric heating by trained person
Arc and electrical hazards: screens, shade, dry PPE
Heavy plate lifting and heat stress; maker's instructions and Centre rules

essays.stem: You lead three welders on a job to weld low-alloy steel crane rail brackets for a wharf in Kingston to an AWS code. Explain how you would plan, run and check the work.
essays.modelAnswer: I would read the drawings and specification, get the approved WPS and check it covers the plate grade, thickness, positions and electrodes. I would check each welder's qualification covers the work and positions. I would check the plate heat numbers against the mill certificates and keep alloy plate marked and apart from mild steel. Electrodes would be issued from a holding oven, with a log. I would brief the team on preheat, interpass and heat input limits, the welding sequence and the safety rules. During the work I would check preheat before tacking and welding, interpass between passes, current and voltage, and cleaning. Each bracket's welds would be numbered on a weld map with the welder, electrode lot and temperatures. After the waiting time set in the plan, I would arrange visual and crack testing. Any defect would be recorded, repaired to procedure and re-tested before the brackets are released.
markingPoints: Reads drawings and specification; confirms WPS and welder qualifications
Material and electrode control (heat numbers, holding oven, log)
Team briefing on limits, sequence and safety
In-process checks of preheat, interpass, settings, cleaning
Weld map and records; delayed inspection, repairs and re-test before release

practical1.title: Vertical-up (3G) single-V butt test plates in low-alloy steel, with preheat, heat input records and bend tests
practical1.brief: Your group is given a WPS for MMAW of a single-V butt joint in low-alloy steel plate (about 10–12 mm) on a backing strip, welded vertical-up (3G), with low-hydrogen alloy electrodes from the holding oven. If the Centre has no low-alloy plate, the assessor gives carbon steel plate and the group works exactly as if it were alloy. Together, read the WPS and write a short plan: the preheat and how it will be checked, the interpass limit, the heat input range, the order in which members weld, and who records. Each member checks the plate marking, prepares and fits one plate on its backing, preheats it and checks it with a crayon or contact thermometer, then welds it uphill. While one member welds, another records the current, voltage, run length and time of each pass and the interpass temperature, and works out the heat input. After the waiting time the assessor sets, each member visually inspects another member's plate. Where the Centre has a bend jig, strips are cut and bent with the assessor; otherwise they are prepared and kept for the assessor.
materials: WPS for MMAW of a 3G single-V butt on low-alloy plate (from the assessor)
Pairs of low-alloy steel plates bevelled to the WPS, with backing strips of the steel the WPS names
Low-hydrogen alloy electrodes to the WPS, kept in a holding oven
MMAW set, with a clamp meter or arc display
Gas preheating burner or heating equipment, with temperature crayons or a contact thermometer
Stopwatch, steel rule, grinder, chipping hammer and wire brush
Weld record sheet with columns for heat input
Bend jig, if the Centre has one
photos: The plan and the WPS limits written on the record sheet
A plate fitted on its backing with the root opening being measured
Preheat being checked with a crayon or thermometer
Each finished cap, with the plate's mark
The completed record sheet with heat input worked out for each pass
checklist: Checked the plate marking and the electrode class against the WPS
Prepared the bevels and fitted the plate on the backing with the correct opening
Preheated evenly and checked the temperature before tacking and welding
Welded uphill with a short arc, weave within the WPS width, cleaning every pass
Kept the interpass temperature within the WPS range
Recorded the pass data and worked out the heat input correctly
Finished cap free of cracks, with no undercut or cap height beyond the limits
safety: Treat preheated plate as hot: mark it, use tongs and heat-resistant gloves
Check the gas burner hoses and arrestors; keep hoses away from the hot plate
Use fume extraction at the arc and read the electrode SDS
Wear full PPE and keep gloves dry
Bend tests only with the jig's guards in place and the assessor present

practical2.title: Plan from mill certificates, then weld an overhead (4G) butt in low-alloy plate and check it with a macro section
practical2.brief: The assessor gives the group two mill certificates for low-alloy plate and a preheat table. As a group, work out the carbon equivalent (CE) of each plate, choose the plate the job will use, read the preheat for its thickness from the table and draft a one-page WPS for an overhead (4G) single-V butt on a backing strip: electrode class and sizes, current range, preheat, interpass limit, heat input limit and pass plan. The assessor checks the draft before welding starts. Then weld two test plates in the 4G position: on each plate, members take turns at the root, fill and cap passes so that every member welds overhead, and the others check the preheat and interpass and record the data. After the waiting time, inspect the caps visually, then saw a cross-section from each plate, file, sand and etch it with the etchant the Centre approves, and mark any defects. Hand in the CE working, the draft WPS, the records and the etched sections.
materials: Two mill certificates and a preheat table (from the assessor)
Low-alloy plates (or carbon steel as a stand-in) bevelled for a single-V butt, with backing strips
Low-hydrogen alloy electrodes in a holding oven
MMAW set with an overhead positioning stand
Heating equipment and temperature crayons or a contact thermometer
Bandsaw, files, abrasive paper and an approved etchant with its SDS
Calculator, WPS form and record sheets
photos: The CE working and the draft WPS
Plates set up in the 4G position with preheat being checked
A member welding overhead in full PPE
The etched cross-sections with any defects marked
checklist: Worked out the CE correctly from the mill certificate
Chose the preheat from the table for the right thickness and CE
Wrote a WPS draft with all the main variables
Welded overhead with small, even beads and no sag
Checked preheat and interpass and recorded the pass data
Prepared the macro section safely and read it correctly
Took a full share of the planning, welding and checking
safety: Wear a flame-resistant cap, closed collar and done-up sleeves for overhead welding
Treat preheated plate as hot and fence the area
Use fume extraction at the arc
Handle the etchant with gloves and goggles as the SDS says, in a ventilated place
Keep guards on the bandsaw and grinder
